title: Low-dropout linear regulator with PMOS pass transistor and single-stage error amplifier
topology: Series-pass linear regulator: a PMOS power transistor operated in the linear/triode region as the pass device, its source tied to the unregulated input rail and its drain driving the regulated output node. A single-stage error amplifier (differential-pair OTA) compares a resistive-divider-scaled sample of the output voltage to a fixed reference (e.g. a bandgap) and drives the pass device's gate to close the loop. PMOS is preferred over an NMOS pass device for low dropout because the error amplifier only needs to pull the gate toward ground (below the source/Vin rail) to fully enhance the device, requiring no gate-drive voltage above Vin and hence no charge pump, unlike an NMOS pass device which needs Vgs above Vin near dropout.
spec_class: power management — regulated, low-noise supply rail for analog/mixed-signal sub-blocks (PLL/VCO supplies, ADC/DAC analog rails, bias reference buffering) sourced from a noisier or higher-voltage upstream rail (battery, switching pre-regulator output) with a small headroom (dropout) budget

pdk_portability.notes: The topology and stability analysis are process-independent, but the achievable dropout voltage and pass-device sizing depend on sky130's PMOS on-resistance-per-micron and safe current-density limits (electromigration rules for the power MOSFET's source/drain routing), so the pass-device width must be re-sized from sky130 SPICE models rather than reused from another process. The output capacitor's required ESR range for stability (see sizing_approach) is also process- and package-independent in principle but must be re-verified against whatever output capacitor technology (ceramic vs. tantalum, on-chip vs. off-chip) is available in the target application, since ESR is a capacitor-technology property, not a PDK property.

sizing_approach: This is inherently a two-pole feedback system and its stability strategy is the central design decision. Pole 1 sits at the error amplifier's output / pass-device gate node, which is high impedance because the pass device presents a large gate capacitance (a wide power PMOS has correspondingly large Cgs+Cgd); this pole's frequency is set by the error-amp's output resistance times the pass-gate capacitance and is largely load-independent. Pole 2 sits at the regulated output node, set by the load resistance (which varies over orders of magnitude with load current) in parallel with the output capacitor; this pole moves with load current, which is what makes LDO compensation hard. The classic external-capacitor strategy (used in the cited work) relies on the output capacitor's own equivalent series resistance (ESR) to introduce a left-half-plane zero that cancels pole 2 over a specified ESR range (e.g. 0.1-3 ohm for a typical off-chip ceramic/tantalum cap), making pole 1 the dominant pole and pole 2+zero a pole-zero doublet that does not erode phase margin as long as ESR stays in range; the error amp's transconductance and pass-device W/L are then sized so pole 1's frequency, together with the guaranteed ESR-zero cancellation, gives at least 45 degrees of phase margin across the full load-current range (including no-load, where pole 2 is slowest). Quiescent current in the error amp and feedback divider is sized as a tradeoff: higher error-amp bias current pushes pole 1 out (improving stability margin and transient response) at the cost of static supply current, which matters directly for battery-powered or capless applications where the LDO's own quiescent draw is a spec-class constraint. For capless (no external ESR available) variants, the alternative strategy is to add an internal buffer stage between the error amp and pass gate and apply Miller compensation across it, trading a design-time capacitor for the reliance on external ESR.
layout_idioms: pass transistor built as a large multi-finger power PMOS with matched finger widths and shared source/drain diffusion strips to spread current density evenly and minimize electromigration risk
thick top-metal routing (or multiple parallel metal layers stitched with vias) for the pass device's source and drain busses to keep IR drop small relative to the regulation accuracy target
feedback-divider resistors laid out as matched unit-resistor strings with common-centroid or symmetric placement so the Vout/Vref ratio is insensitive to process gradients across the divider

four-terminal (Kelvin) sensing of the regulated output node for the feedback tap, routed separately from the high-current output bus, so IR drop in the power routing does not appear as a DC regulation error

guard ring around the pass transistor and error amplifier tied to a quiet substrate/well tap to block switching noise injected by the (typically noisier) upstream supply domain from coupling into the regulated output

source.citation: G. A. Rincon-Mora and P. E. Allen, "A low-voltage, low quiescent current, low drop-out regulator," IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, vol. 33, no. 1, pp. 36-44, Jan. 1998.
source.license_or_openness: Peer-reviewed IEEE journal paper cited here for its pass-device/error-amp topology and ESR-zero compensation methodology only (no figures or text reproduced), per the KB's open-sources sourcing rule. This is the foundational, most widely cited published analysis of PMOS-pass-device LDO stability via output-capacitor ESR, and essentially all subsequent LDO literature (including capless variants) frames its compensation strategy against this paper's pole/zero analysis.

notes: Framed here as the baseline external-capacitor PMOS-pass LDO; capless (on-chip-only output capacitor) variants replace the ESR-zero reliance with an internal buffer stage and Miller compensation, trading quiescent current and design complexity for the ability to drop the external component, and are a natural follow-up KB entry if a capless design becomes relevant to a spec_class target. The dropout voltage floor for this topology is set by the PMOS pass device's Vds(sat)/on-resistance at the maximum load current, not by any bandgap-related Vbe drop, which is what makes it compatible with sub-1.8V rails when paired with a sub-1V reference such as the current-summing bandgap in kb/entries/sky130-bandgap-reference.json.
